# How to Find Your Color Season With ChatGPT Using Words, Not Photos

> **In short:** You can describe your veins, jewelry test and hair and eye colors to ChatGPT in plain sentences, then ask for a color-season guess and a checklist to confirm it in daylight. The key limit: ChatGPT cannot see you, so its guess is only as good as your description.

Color seasons are a popular way to sort colors into palettes that tend to flatter different people, often grouped as spring, summer, autumn and winter. In this guide you will describe yourself in words, ask ChatGPT for a likely season and its reasons, and build a short list of daylight tests to check the result yourself. No photos are needed, and you don't need any experience with AI.

## Before you start

- **An OpenAI account and access to ChatGPT.** Use the website or the mobile app. The free version works for this task, though limits on how many messages you can send may apply.
- **A window with natural daylight.** You will need this for the veins check and the final confirmation.
- **About 20 to 30 minutes.** Most of the time goes to looking at your wrist and holding up clothes.

## Step 1 — Open a fresh chat

Open ChatGPT in your browser or app and start a new chat. You should see an empty conversation with a message box at the bottom of the screen. If you can't find a way to start a new chat, look for a button or pencil-style icon that says something like "New chat", usually near the top or along the side. It's best to use a fresh chat so your earlier conversations don't affect the answer.

Click into the message box. It may be labeled with a short hint such as "Message" or "Ask anything," though your version may use different words. You don't need to type anything yet, but you should see a blinking cursor once you tap or click inside it.

You'll know it worked when you have an empty chat and a cursor is blinking inside the message box at the bottom.

## Step 2 — Describe your veins in plain words

Go to a window with daylight, not a lamp. Turn your inner wrist face-up and look at the veins. Decide whether they look more blue or purple, or more green or olive. If you can't tell, that's useful too. Write down what you see in your own words.

Now type your observation into the message box and press the send button (usually an arrow icon, or the Enter key on a computer). Your message appears on the screen, and ChatGPT starts writing its answer below it, one line at a time.

If the answer seems to skip your observation, that's normal early on. Just keep going, because the next steps add more detail.

💬 Example: "In natural daylight my inner wrist veins look [blue-purple or green-olive], and I can't tell for sure."

You'll know it worked when ChatGPT replies and mentions your veins in its answer.

## Step 3 — Describe your jewelry test

Next, describe how you look in silver versus gold. Hold a silver piece and then a gold piece near your face in daylight, or imagine them if you don't own any. Notice which one makes your skin look brighter and which one makes it look dull or yellowish. Write down which metal you prefer and why.

Type a message that covers that comparison. Be honest about what you see, because the guess depends on your words. ChatGPT's answer will usually mention undertones, which is the subtle warm or cool tint under your skin. If the answer uses a word you don't know, ask it to explain. Ask a follow-up question in the same chat.

If you aren't sure which metal looks better, say so. A message like "I can't decide" is still helpful, and the tool can weigh that into its guess.

💬 Example: "Silver makes my face look [brighter or duller], and gold makes it look [warmer or yellowish], so I think I prefer [silver or gold]."

You'll know it worked when ChatGPT responds with a note about your undertone, such as warm, cool or neutral.

## Step 4 — Describe your natural hair and eye colors

Now add the easy details. Write your natural hair color as it was in childhood or as it is without dye, and your eye color in plain words. Include any change over time, such as hair that has darkened or grayed. If you color your hair, mention the shade you started with, not the dye you use now.

Send this information in a message of its own. Keep it factual, and don't add guesses about how you "should" look. The more clearly you describe your natural coloring, the easier it is for ChatGPT to match you to a palette.

If you're unsure about your eye color because it looks different in different light, describe both shades you see. That gives the answer better material to work with.

💬 Example: "My natural hair color is [dark brown or blonde or red], and my eyes look [hazel or blue or brown] in daylight."

You'll know it worked when ChatGPT responds with a season guess that refers to your hair and eye details.

## Step 5 — Ask for a season guess with reasons

Now ask directly for a guess, and ask for the reasoning too. A good request includes the four common seasons, so the answer stays focused. Ask ChatGPT to list the two or three points that influenced its guess and to say which points are uncertain. This matters, because a guess with its reasons is easier to check than a bare label.

Look for the answer below your message. Read the reasons slowly. If one reason is based on something you didn't tell the tool, tell it so in your next message and ask for a revised guess.

If the answer seems to hedge too much, ask: "What would change your answer?" That question often brings out the most useful details.

💬 Example: "Based on everything I've told you, which of the four seasons fits me best? Please list the reasons and tell me which parts are uncertain."

You'll know it worked when you get one main season, a short list of reasons and a note about what is uncertain.

## Step 6 — Ask for a daylight checklist

Last, ask ChatGPT for a short list of questions you can answer yourself in daylight. This is where you confirm or challenge the guess. Good questions compare how your face looks next to different fabrics, such as a bright white versus a soft cream, or a cool blue versus a warm orange. Ask the tool to phrase each question so you can answer "yes," "no," or "not sure."

Then do the tests. Hold each fabric under your chin in daylight, and look at a mirror. Write your answers. Return to the chat and type them in, then ask whether the season guess still fits. ChatGPT only knows what you tell it, so your answers are what it will use to refine the guess.

💬 Example: "Give me five yes-or-no questions I can answer in daylight, comparing [color one] and [color two] held under my chin."

You'll know it worked when you have a numbered list of questions and you can answer each one by looking in a mirror.

## Common mistakes

- **Trusting the first guess as final.** A single word-based answer is a starting point, not a verdict. Fix it by completing the daylight checklist and reporting your results back to the chat.
- **Testing under lamps or screens.** Warm indoor light and phone glare change how colors look. Fix it by testing near a window in daylight, and avoid direct sun on your face.
- **Forgetting ChatGPT can't see you.** It cannot judge your skin, and it does not know what you look like unless you describe it. Fix it by giving clear, honest descriptions and treating the output as a guide, not a diagnosis.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** Use your season result when shopping for clothes, makeup or a paint color for a room. Start with a few pieces and see how often you reach for them.
- **For your business or work:** If you help clients choose colors for a presentation, logo or event, you can use the same approach to draft a list of questions for a client to answer in daylight.
- **If you're just getting started:** Begin with the veins check and the silver-versus-gold comparison. Those two answers alone give ChatGPT enough to make a useful first guess.

## Try it now

Open a new chat, then type one sentence describing what your veins look like in daylight. Read the reply and notice whether it mentions your undertone. That single exchange is the whole method in miniature, and you can keep building from there.
